On first boot, Omarchy invites you to set up a default agent. Pick your favorite, sign in, and put it to work on your computer.
When an app crashes, click the notification to send your agent on the case. It can examine the crash dump, diagnose what went wrong, and help report the bug.

Critic: Omarchy is no longer an install script, so you download a 7GB ISO that ships with Zoom, Spotify, Hey, Basecamp, Steam, Minecraft, etc., yet still uses Arch's package mirrors. It's neither a lightweight script like LARBS nor a true derivative like EndeavourOS or Manjaro.
Downloading the Omarchy 3 ISO last week was painfully slow, sitting at about 600 KiB/s.

Security report: Omarchy configured its default user as a member of the docker group, letting any user process escalate to root. Docker's own docs warn this is unsafe, and Omarchy made it the default without telling users.
Commenter notes a recent fix where Omarchy was passing USB descriptors straight into the shell (commit 9285b19), and calls it a sign of a vibecoded distro.
Omarchy plugins (plugins.omarchy.org) run completely unsandboxed and unvetted, and someone should audit them.
Defender: the Docker configuration issue was reported and changed quickly, which shows the system working. Omarchy is a simple way to test drive Hyprland and write code.
Omarchy is the first distro that 'stuck' for me. I've used it on my desktop for a year for personal projects and light Steam gaming. Previous attempts with Ubuntu and Pop!_OS never stuck.

Blog post criticism: there are 'bangers like video title bash injection or all notifications being able to run arbitrary bash on your machine.' Commenters blame Omarchy relying on large amounts of bash scripting.

A friend urged me for months, and I finally installed Omarchy after a horrible experience with CachyOS. I understand the hype: it works, the install is uncomplicated with no bootloader or WM choices, the tiling matches how I use my Mac, and installing software is easy and lightning-fast.
When I first tried it I was annoyed by the bloat and the promotion of their own software. I heard an option to remove the bloat was added later, but I won't try it again.
Wish: I would love for the Omarchy shell to be distro-agnostic, just dotfiles and binaries you could copy to any distro that has the required software.
Hyprland in Omarchy was too far from what I'm used to and required too many workflow changes. But DHH's push convinced me to try daily-driving Linux, so I'm switching to Fedora/GNOME.
Omarchy 2.0 ships as an Arch-based ISO, and installation is fairly quick (~5 minutes on a fresh machine) given decent bandwidth.
I want to love Omarchy, but replacing the boot splash screen with its logo is rough, and there's no clear way to disable it.

I like Omarchy but settled on CachyOS + Hyprland with ML4W dotfiles for the kernel optimizations and Fish. I wish DHH would separate the Hyprland config so I could try it on an existing Arch setup, since Hyprland doesn't work well in VMs.

I've tried to set up Arch with Hyprland three times on my own and with the most popular dotfiles. It was terrible, frustrating, and things broke constantly. Omarchy fixed that and I can't recommend it enough.

Installed Omarchy on a €30 N23 Chromebook with a 32GB SSD. The ISO route failed and I fell back to archinstall, but it's the greatest out-of-the-box Linux experience I've had. Easy to mod: I changed the battery indicator to show wattage with a one-line change.
I tried it and felt the same as the author: it's just ricing, an opinionated layer of dotfiles on top of Arch.
Workaround: install Omarchy, read the repo to see how the parts you liked were set up, then install Arch or Cachy and reuse just those parts.
The new Quickshell-based Omarchy shell is already an excellent foundation. Omarchy has excellent defaults, and development keeps moving in the right direction.
